text: (a) Τὸ ἡμέτερον ἑκουσίως προσχωρήσωμεν. Active accepit Turrianus, cum ita reddit, Eam quæ nostra est, sponte ad Deum accommodemus. Ubi is, qui Baronianæ editioni præfuit, sive is ipse, non bene margini apposuit, Fort. quod nostrum est, τὸ ἡμέτερον enim, θέλημα, refert : ac bene Turrianus expressit : eam, quæ nostra est, id est, voluntas : nec hic scrupulus est, sed quod ex vet. leg. τὸ προσχωρήσωμεν activum fecit, quod nunquam aliter quam neutrum usurpari videtur. Locus quem affert vet. lex, incerto auctore, huic nostro geminus est. Προσκεχωρήκασιν τὴν γλῶσσαν πρὸς τὸ Καρικὸν ἔθνος : Accommodaverunt, aptaverunt linguam, etc. At melius Steph. γλῶσσαν accipit, pro, κατὰ γλῶσσαν, ecclipsi Græcis consuetissima, et sic erit idem ac λόγῳ, sermone, lingua, accesserunt. Hic vero Nostra voluntate sponte accedamus ; nos Deo, quasi dedititii, sponte submittamus.
anchorLine: ῥον ἑκουσίως προσχωρήσωμεν (a) τῷ Θεῷ, ἐκ τοῦ
en: Our own will freely go over to (accede to) God. Turrianus took this actively, translating 'Let us accommodate that which is ours, of its own accord, to God.' Whoever supervised the Baronian edition (or Baronius himself) wrongly put in the margin 'Perhaps: that which is ours', since τὸ ἡμέτερον refers to θέλημα (will); and Turrianus rendered it well: 'that which is ours', that is, the will. Nor is there a difficulty here, except that, following an old reading, he made προσχωρήσωμεν active, which never seems to be used other than as a neuter. The passage that the old lexicon cites, from an unnamed author, is a twin of this one: 'They have attached their tongue to the Carian people', that is, 'They have accommodated, fitted, their tongue', and so on. But Stephanus better takes γλῶσσαν as standing for 'according to tongue', an ellipsis very common in Greek, and so it will be the same as 'by speech, by language, they have come over'. Here, however, it is 'Let us come over by our own will, of our own accord'; let us submit ourselves to God of our own accord, like those who have surrendered.

text: (b) Κατὰ τοῦτο ἐκλείψει. Non extant eo psalmo hæc Basilii verba, nisi Maximus ejus habuit pleniorem ἔκδοσιν, vel ex memoria citavit, sibique Basilii textum conflavit ex iis, quæ illo psal. et quæ Isa. VII, in ejus expositione legerat. Ad hunc sensum igitur exponit Basil. p. 259, non Isaiæ locum, sed ejus psalmi versum, Dilexisti justitiam, et odisti iniquitatem, quod reliqui homines labore et exercitatione, prona ad bonum malumque voluntate, ægre tandem impleant : Σοὶ δὲ φυσική τίς ἐστι πρὸς τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἡ οἰκείωσις, καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀνομίαν ἀλλοίωσις. Tibi ad bonum naturalis necessitudo, et ab improbitate aversio, οἰκείωσις, naturalis proprietas, quod reddit interp. rudius est. Fusius dicto cap. 7, p. 1007, ubi nostris sic ad utrumque pronis, opponit. Ἀλλ' οὐχὶ καὶ ὁ Κύριος οὕτως, ἀλλ' ἡ πρὸς τὸ ἀγαθὸν αὐτοῦ οἰκείωσις, εὐθὺς ἐκ πρώτης γενέσεως διεφαίνετο. Τί γὰρ γέγραπται; « Ὅτι πρὶν ἢ γνῶναι αὐτὸν ἢ προελέσθαι πονηρὰ, ἐκλέξεται ἀγαθόν. At non sic etiam Dominus, sed ejus ad bonum necessitudo, a primo statim ortu elucescebat. Quid enim scriptum est? Antequam sciat ipse, aut præeligat mala, eliget bona. Ubi turbate interpr. Titelm. et laciniose, Sed quod erat bonum sibi vindicabat, familiariter etiam initio statim et a primordio suæ nativitatis in ipso inclaruit ; quibus nec fidem interpr. nec bonæ lucem paraph. affert. Quare illud, τὸ γὰρ πρὶν ἢ, δηλοῖ, non Basilii expositio est, ut Turr. existimavit, sive qui Baronianæ editioni præfuit, sed Maximi, Basilii verba et Isaiæ, magis explicantis.
anchorLine: Κατὰ τοῦτο ἐκλείψει (b)
en: 'According to this he will fail.' These words of Basil are not extant in that psalm, unless Maximus had a fuller edition of it, or cited from memory and put together for himself a text of Basil from what he had read in Basil's exposition of that psalm and of Isaiah 7. In this sense, then, Basil (p. 259) expounds not the passage of Isaiah but the verse of that psalm, 'Thou hast loved justice and hated iniquity', which other men, with a will inclined to good and evil by labour and exercise, fulfil only with difficulty: 'To thee there is a natural affinity (oikeiosis) to the good and an alteration away from iniquity.' The rendering 'natural necessity for the good, and aversion from wickedness, oikeiosis, natural property' by the interpreter is cruder. He argues more fully in the cited chapter 7, p. 1007, where he sets this against our people being thus inclined to both. 'But not so the Lord, but his affinity to the good shone forth immediately from his first coming into being. For what is written? Before he knows, or chooses evil, he will choose good.' Where the interpreter Titelman, in a confused and rambling way, has 'But what was good he claimed for himself, and familiarly even from the very beginning and from the first origin of his birth it shone forth in him'; which neither lends credit to the interpreter nor light to the paraphrast. Therefore the phrase 'for before' (to gar prin e) makes clear that this is not Basil's exposition, as Turrianus thought, or whoever supervised the Baronian edition, but Maximus's, explaining the words of Basil and of Isaiah.
